experience.role: Graduate Researcher, Personalized AI for Health
experience.summary: Wearable sensing is noisy and deployment is constrained, so I built multimodal pipelines and personalized models that stay interpretable on device and useful across users.
experience.detail: This is the work that made modeling, evaluation, and deployment constraints feel like one problem instead of separate phases.

bullets.text: Wearable force estimation needed a smaller baseline, so I led SER and showed low-rank models could match or beat heavier LSTMs while staying interpretable and credible for edge deployment.

Research pipelines were fragmented across sensing modalities, so I built end-to-end data, training, and evaluation workflows that made comparison under noise and subject shift reliable enough to guide model decisions.
One-size-fits-all models broke across users, so I framed personalization around latency, privacy, and federated adaptation to keep the system deployable instead of trapped in a lab setting.

experience.summary: Ranking gains had to survive real traffic and strong baselines, so I built production-constrained model and evaluation workflows that made improvements worth trusting.
experience.detail: The ranking work sharpened my judgment for strong baselines, traffic heterogeneity, and the difference between a better model and a misleading evaluation.

bullets.text: Multi-objective ranking needed more selective capacity, so I designed Transformer MoE models that fused text and structured signals and created a scalable path to specialization.
Traffic heterogeneity kept breaking naive expert routing, so I built distributed training and evaluation loops that preserved specialization gains under capacity limits and shifting demand.
Model novelty can hide weak measurement, so I carried research-style evaluation discipline into ranking and kept decisions tied to operationally realistic metrics the team could trust.

experience.summary: Real-time analytics depended on trustworthy ingestion, so I owned a Kafka-to-ClickHouse pipeline that kept data correct through exactly-once behavior and safer operations.
experience.detail: This was hands-on systems work below the model layer, where interfaces, schema evolution, and failure recovery decide whether a platform is dependable.

bullets.text: Multi-datacenter ingestion risked duplicate or dropped events, so I integrated Kafka Connector into ClickHouse with exactly-once semantics and made streaming analytics safer to trust.
Upgrades and schema changes could break downstream consumers, so I hardened rollout and evolution paths to keep the pipeline operable across environments instead of brittle during change.

experience.summary: Production clusters need upgrades and debugging to be boring, so I shipped Kubernetes platform features and CI tooling that made operations safer and easier to trust.
experience.detail: OpenShift taught me to treat release safety, interoperability, and debuggability as product features, not cleanup work.

bullets.text: Operator installs and upgrades were fragile at cluster scale, so I owned OLM changes for dependency resolution, upgrade safety, and version orchestration that made cluster rollouts safer.
Distributed build failures obscured real regressions, so I built statistical flake detection that made CI output faster to trust and faster to debug.
Ecosystem integration slowed teams adopting operators, so I led Helm and Operator Framework integration and widened the path for interoperability across tools.

experience.summary: Resource sharing across clouds is hard to trust, so I modeled QoS and incentive constraints to show when federation actually improves system utility and adoption.
experience.detail: This line of work keeps showing up in how I think about multi-tenant ML systems: the policy and incentive layer matters as much as raw performance.

bullets.text: Hybrid-cloud federation can shift load without helping users, so I built a queueing framework that identified when QoS-constrained sharing improves utility enough to be worth deploying.
Decentralized partners need fair incentives to cooperate, so I added Shapley-based allocation that made federation harder to game and easier for partners to adopt.

projects.name: Operator Lifecycle Manager
projects.summary: Cluster upgrades are easy to break, so I contributed to OLM to manage dependency-aware installs and safer lifecycle orchestration on OpenShift clusters.
projects.detail: Strong proof of production systems judgment: upgrades, dependency graphs, and ecosystem interoperability all mattered at once.

projects.name: Flake Analyzer
projects.summary: Flaky CI hides real regressions, so I built statistical detection and classification tooling that made distributed test failures faster to trust and debug.
projects.detail: Useful proof that I care about reliability loops and developer throughput, not just core product code.

projects.name: SER
projects.summary: Wearable GRF estimation needed a lighter baseline, so I implemented SER and showed interpretable low-rank modeling could stay accurate enough for deployment-minded biomechanics work.
projects.detail: SVD embeddings and lightweight regression keep the model inspectable, efficient, and realistic for on-device biomechanics.

projects.name: CoT-Rec
projects.summary: Chain-of-thought generation is noisy, so I turned reasoning traces into ranking candidates and improved final selection with reranking instead of trusting decode order.
projects.detail: Multiple reasoning traces become candidates that can be scored, ranked, and selected instead of accepted in generation order.

projects.name: Shapley Value Calculator
projects.summary: Shared systems need incentives people will accept, so I packaged Shapley allocation into reusable code that turns fairness arguments into concrete payouts teams can use.
projects.detail: Shapley value turns fairness in shared-resource systems into a concrete allocation rule instead of a vague intuition.

projects.name: RCDS_GO
projects.summary: Large remote states are expensive to resync, so I implemented content-aware reconciliation that sends differences instead of whole payloads and makes huge-file sync more practical.
projects.detail: Efficient reconciliation is useful anywhere synchronization is expensive, from distributed hosts to biological sequences and potentially future model-state transfer.

publications.title: Estimating Ground Reaction Forces From Inertial Sensors

signal.resume-engineering: Wearable force estimation faced deployment limits, and this paper shows a lighter model can stay accurate enough to be useful in practice.
signal.resume-embodied-ml: Ground-reaction estimation from IMUs is noisy and resource-constrained, and this paper shows SER can stay interpretable, lightweight, and credible outside the lab.
signal.resume-advanced-ml: Sequence models are not always right, and this paper shows honest evaluation can favor a smaller architecture with clearer behavior.

publications.title: Performance and Revenue Analysis of Hybrid Cloud Federations with QoS Requirements
publications.authors: Bowen Song, Marco Paolieri, Leana Golubchik

signal.resume-engineering: Hybrid cloud sharing is hard to size and trust, and this paper provides a QoS and incentive model for deciding when federation is worth deploying.
signal.resume-embodied-ml: Deployable ML inherits systems constraints, and this paper shows the resource and incentive reasoning behind how I think about scaling under limits.
signal.resume-advanced-ml: Optimization alone is not enough, and this paper connects performance analysis to incentives and the tradeoffs operators actually face.

publications.title: Scalable String Reconciliation by Recursive Content-Dependent Shingling

signal.resume-engineering: Synchronizing large remote states is bandwidth-heavy, and this paper introduces a reconciliation method that performs well on real revision histories and large files.
signal.resume-embodied-ml: I treat algorithms as things to implement and benchmark, and this paper shows that pattern on a difficult synchronization problem with real constraints.
signal.resume-advanced-ml: Theory mattered here, but so did realistic validation, and that same standard carries into my applied ML work and model evaluation.
